Sandars, N. K. (trans.). *The Epic of Gilgamesh* (Penguin Classics, 1960, rev. 1972) — earlier widely read translation.

temples: No attested cult site; Utnapishtim was not worshipped as a god
worship.practices: Utnapishtim received no cult and was not an object of worship; his significance is entirely literary, as the sole mortal granted the immortality that Gilgamesh, and by extension every human reader, ultimately cannot obtain.

name: Mictecacihuatl

originalLanguageName.meaning: Lady of the Dead

description: Queen of Mictlan, the Aztec underworld, ruling alongside her husband Mictlantecuhtli over the ninth and deepest level of the land of the dead. Mictecacihuatl presided over the bones of the deceased and the festivals honoring the dead within the Aztec calendar.
detailedBio:
## Lady of the Dead

Mictecacihuatl is the queen of Mictlan, the deepest and final level of the nine-layered Aztec underworld, ruling jointly with her husband Mictlantecuhtli. Spanish friar Bernardino de Sahagun's *Florentine Codex*, compiled from Nahua informants in the 16th century, describes the pair as the great lord and lady presiding over the land of the dead, to whom the souls of most people who died ordinary deaths would eventually travel after a difficult four-year journey through Mictlan's other levels.

### Guardian of Bones

Mictecacihuatl's particular domain within this shared rule was the safekeeping of the bones of the dead, which the Aztecs regarded as essential material for the renewal of life. In the well-known myth of the Fifth Sun's creation, the god Quetzalcoatl travels to Mictlan to retrieve the bones of people from previous world-ages in order to fashion the new humanity, a journey that brings him into contact with the realm over which Mictecacihuatl and her husband preside, though the surviving accounts of this episode center the negotiation on Mictlantecuhtli.

### The Festivals of the Dead

Sahagun's *Florentine Codex* records two major festivals honoring the dead within the Aztec solar calendar: Miccailhuitontli ("the small feast of the dead") in the ninth month, and Hueymiccaílhuitl ("the great feast of the dead") in the tenth month. These precolonial observances are often popularly connected to the modern Día de los Muertos, but the two should not be treated as simply identical: the contemporary holiday is a later colonial-era and modern syncretism of Indigenous Mesoamerican traditions with the Catholic All Saints' and All Souls' Days, and its direct historical relationship to the specific Aztec festivals honoring Mictecacihuatl is more complex than popular accounts often suggest.

### A Feared but Necessary Power

Unlike deities associated with punishment for moral failing, Mictecacihuatl and Mictlantecuhtli's realm awaited most Aztecs regardless of how they had lived; death by drowning, in childbirth, or in battle sent souls to other, distinct afterlife destinations instead. Mictecacihuatl thus represents not judgment but the natural, inevitable end that governed the vast majority of Aztec dead.
originStory: Mictecacihuatl rules Mictlan, the ninth and deepest level of the Aztec underworld, alongside her husband Mictlantecuhtli. According to Sahagun's Florentine Codex, most souls who died ordinary deaths journeyed for four years through Mictlan's upper levels before reaching her and her husband's realm, where she presided over the bones of the dead.

primarySources.text: And the lord of the region of the dead was named Mictlantecutli, and his consort was named Mictecacihuatl.
primarySources.source: Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book 3 (trans. Anderson & Dibble)
primarySources.date: Compiled 1545-1590 CE, from earlier Nahua tradition

furtherReading.note: A related Mesoamerican underworld tradition (Maya) useful for comparative context, though a distinct text from the Aztec sources
Covers Mictecacihuatl's role and the caveats around her popular association with Día de los Muertos

sources: Sahagún, Bernardino de (trans. Arthur J. O. Anderson and Charles E. Dibble). *Florentine Codex: General History of the Things of New Spain* (School of American Research and University of Utah, 1950-1982).
Miller, Mary and Taube, Karl. *An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya* (Thames & Hudson, 1993).

crossPantheonParallels.note: Both are queens who rule the underworld jointly with, or alongside, a consort presiding over the realm of the dead

temples: Honored within broader Mictlan-focused ritual rather than a single dedicated major temple
festivals: Miccailhuitontli (ninth month) and Hueymiccaílhuitl (tenth month), festivals of the dead recorded in the Florentine Codex
worship.practices: Mictecacihuatl was honored jointly with Mictlantecuhtli through calendar festivals dedicated to the dead and through funerary ritual concerned with the fate of the bones and the soul's long journey through Mictlan, rather than through a single grand state temple in her name alone.

name: Ometeotl

originalLanguageName.meaning: Two God, Dual God

description: A primordial dual-gendered creative principle described in some colonial-era Nahua sources as residing in Omeyocan, the highest level of the heavens, and identified with the paired deities Ometecuhtli and Omecihuatl. Whether Ometeotl represents a single, named pre-Columbian deity or is chiefly a later scholarly synthesis of the paired creator gods is a genuinely unresolved debate among specialists.
detailedBio:
## The Dual Principle

Ometeotl, meaning "Two God" or "Dual God," names a primordial, dual-gendered creative force described in a cluster of colonial-era Nahua sources, most notably the anonymous 16th-century Spanish compilation *Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas*, as dwelling in Omeyocan, the thirteenth and highest level of the Aztec heavens. In this account, the dual god, also called Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl ("Lord and Lady of Our Sustenance"), engendered the four Tezcatlipocas — Xipe Totec (the Red Tezcatlipoca), Huitzilopochtli (associated with the Blue Tezcatlipoca in this telling), Quetzalcoatl (the White Tezcatlipoca), and Tezcatlipoca proper (the Black Tezcatlipoca) — who in turn undertook the work of creating the world and the successive Suns (world-ages).

### A Genuinely Contested Concept

Unlike most entries in this catalog, Ometeotl's very status as a coherent, singularly named deity is disputed among scholars of Mesoamerican religion, and that debate deserves to be stated plainly rather than smoothed over. The historian and philosopher Miguel Leon-Portilla, in his influential *Aztec Thought and Culture* (1963), argued that Ometeotl represented a sophisticated, near-monotheistic or panentheistic philosophical current within elite Nahua religious thought, synthesizing the paired creator deities into a single, transcendent dual principle. Other scholars, notably Richard Haly in "Bare Bones: Rethinking Mesoamerican Divinity" (1992), have pushed back forcefully, arguing that the primary colonial-era sources consistently speak of paired deities, Ometecuhtli/Omecihuatl or Tonacatecuhtli/Tonacacihuatl, and that a single deity named simply "Ometeotl" as commonly presented in modern popular and even some scholarly accounts is substantially a 20th-century interpretive construct rather than a term with clear, direct standing in the primary sources.

### The Parent of the Four Tezcatlipocas

Whatever position one takes in that scholarly debate, the underlying mythic material, the paired dual god's generation of the four Tezcatlipoca brothers who go on to shape the world, is well attested in the *Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas* and related texts, and it is on this basis that Ometeotl/Ometecuhtli-Omecihuatl is treated here as the ultimate primordial source of several of the Aztec pantheon's most important gods.
originStory: According to the Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas, the dual creator, dwelling in the highest heaven of Omeyocan and known also as Tonacatecuhtli and Tonacacihuatl, engendered the four Tezcatlipoca brothers, who then undertook the work of shaping the world and its successive ages. Scholars remain divided over whether 'Ometeotl' should be understood as a single named deity in pre-Columbian thought or as a modern synthesis of the paired creator gods.

primarySources.text: This god of theirs had two names, one Tonacatecutli, and the other Tonacacihuatl... and this god was in the thirteenth heaven, where he had his beginning and origin.
primarySources.source: Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas (composite paraphrase, trans. after Garibay)
primarySources.date: Compiled c. 1530s CE, from Nahua informants

furtherReading.note: Covers the scholarly debate over Ometeotl's status as a singular deity concept

sources: Leon-Portilla, Miguel. *Aztec Thought and Culture: A Study of the Ancient Nahuatl Mind* (University of Oklahoma Press, 1963) — the principal argument for Ometeotl as a unified philosophical concept.
Haly, Richard. "Bare Bones: Rethinking Mesoamerican Divinity." *History of Religions* 31, no. 3 (1992) — the principal scholarly challenge to treating Ometeotl as a singular pre-Columbian deity.
Miller, Mary and Taube, Karl. *An Illustrated Dictionary of the Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya* (Thames & Hudson, 1993).

crossPantheonParallels.note: Both are primordial figures whose act of generation stands at the very root of the pantheon's cosmogony, though Ometeotl's dual nature has no close parallel in Pangu's solitary emergence

temples: No securely attested dedicated temple; the associated forms Tonacatecuhtli/Tonacacihuatl were venerated as remote, abstract creators rather than through an active, image-based state cult
worship.practices: Unlike the major gods of the Aztec state cult (Huitzilopochtli, Tezcatlipoca, Tlaloc), the dual creator described in sources like the Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas appears as a remote, largely abstract originating principle rather than a deity with an active, image-centered public cult of temples and festivals.

name: Perun

originalLanguageName.meaning: "The Striker"; from a Proto-Slavic root also seen in Baltic Perkūnas, part of a wider Indo-European thunder-god word family

description: The thunder god of the Kievan Rus', sworn by in treaties and installed at the head of Prince Vladimir's official pantheon in 980 before Vladimir himself had his idol destroyed in 988.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Perun is the best-attested of the Rus' gods. The *Russian Primary Chronicle* has the Rus' swear by him and by their weapons in the treaties of 907 and 945, and again in 971; under 980 he stands first among the six idols Vladimir raises on the hill outside his Kiev palace, with a head of silver and a moustache of gold. Procopius, writing in the 550s, describes the early Slavs sacrificing cattle to an unnamed god who alone is "master of all" and "the maker of lightning" — not a named source for Perun, but read by most historians as the same figure centuries earlier.

## A prince's god, then a discarded one

Perun's cult is closely tied to the Rus' ruling class and its armed retinue: the oaths he witnesses are sworn between princes and states. In 988, after Vladimir converts to Christianity, the chronicle has his idol dragged behind a horse, beaten, and thrown into the Dnieper — a deliberate, public undoing of the very installation of 980. The often-repeated tale of a running combat between Perun and Veles is not in any medieval text; it is a modern scholarly reconstruction (see the entry on Veles).

crossPantheonParallels.note: Both are hammer/axe-wielding thunder gods invoked in oaths, part of the wider Indo-European storm-god pattern; Perun's name is directly cognate with Baltic Perkūnas, Thor's closest attested parallel outside Scandinavia.

Ivanov and Toporov's reconstruction of a Perun-vs-serpent combat draws its structure from the Vedic Indra-vs-Vritra myth, part of the comparative case for a shared Indo-European storm-god-versus-serpent motif.

primarySources.text: And Igor summoned the [Byzantine] envoys, and went to the hill where Perun stood, and they laid down their arms, their shields, and their gold, and swore oaths.
primarySources.source: Russian Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (paraphrase of the treaty oath)
primarySources.date: entry for 945 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

primarySources.text: And Vladimir set up idols on the hill outside the palace: Perun of wood with a head of silver and a moustache of gold, and Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh.
primarySources.date: entry for 980 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

temples: No enclosed temple building is attested for Perun among the East Slavs; worship was in the open air. An excavated horseshoe-shaped ditch and central post-pit at Peryn, near Novgorod, is widely interpreted by archaeologists as a Perun sanctuary, matching the First Novgorod Chronicle's report that Bishop Akim had Perun's idol thrown into the Volkhov there in 989.
worship.practices: Oaths of state were sworn on Perun's name alongside weapons (907, 945, 971 treaties). Procopius describes cattle and other animals sacrificed to the Slavs' supreme thunder-god in general terms. In later East Slavic folklore, Perun's thunder role and his midsummer date were partly absorbed into the feast of the prophet Elijah (Ilyin Den) — a post-Christian folk continuation, not a pagan-era practice.

name: Veles

originalLanguageName.meaning: Etymology disputed; possibly related to Slavic *vol- ("ox") given his epithet, or to a root shared with Baltic Velinas/Vels, a spirit of the dead

description: The "cattle god" (skotii bog) of the treaty oaths, sworn by beside Perun in 907 and 945, and left off Vladimir's 980 hilltop pantheon in a way scholars have long puzzled over.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

The *Russian Primary Chronicle* has the Rus' swear by Volos, "the cattle god" (*skotii bog*), together with Perun and their weapons, in the treaties of 907 and 945. Unlike Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh, Veles is conspicuously absent from the six idols Vladimir sets up on the Kiev hill in 980. Later medieval and early-modern hagiographic tradition associated with Vladimir's baptism places a Veles idol separately, on the lower ground of the Podil district by the river — a detail that postdates the Primary Chronicle itself and should be treated with more caution than the 907 and 945 treaty text.

## A modern reconstruction, clearly labelled

The absence of Veles from the hill, and his separate association with lower/wet ground, underlies Vyacheslav Ivanov and Vladimir Toporov's influential 1974 reconstruction of a cosmic conflict between a sky-based Perun and an earth- or water-based Veles, echoing comparable Indo-European storm-god-versus-serpent combats (Indra/Vritra, Thor/Jörmungandr). No medieval Slavic text narrates this combat; it is inferred from later folk tales, place names, and comparative mythology, and is presented on this site strictly as a scholarly reconstruction. Later folklore also associates Veles with poetry, magic, and (via the 12th-century *Tale of Igor's Campaign*, which calls the poet Boyan "Veles's grandson") skilled speech, though the *Tale*'s own authenticity as an unaltered 12th-century text has been debated by some scholars.

primarySources.text: Let those who break this oath [...] be cursed by God in whom they believe, and by Perun and Volos, the cattle god.
primarySources.source: Russian Primary Chronicle, s.a. 907 (paraphrase of the treaty oath)
primarySources.date: entry for 907 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

primarySources.text: And the Rus' who are not baptized lay down their shields and their naked swords [...] swearing for themselves and for all Rus' by Perun their god, and Volos, the god of cattle.
primarySources.source: Russian Primary Chronicle, s.a. 945 (paraphrase of the treaty oath)
primarySources.date: entry for 945 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

worship.practices: Sworn by merchants and traders alongside Perun in the state treaties of 907 and 945, distinct from any temple cult recorded for him. Later East Slavic folk practice partly transferred his patronage of cattle and wealth to Saint Blaise (Vlasiy), whose feast day (11 February, Old Style) was kept as a blessing of livestock — a post-Christian folk continuation, not a pagan-era rite.

name: Mokosh

originalLanguageName.meaning: Disputed: possibly from Slavic *mok- ("moist", suggesting a moist-earth mother figure), or a borrowing of the ethnonym of the Finnic Moksha people, whose territory neighbored the early Rus'

description: The only goddess among Vladimir's six idols of 980, later folk memory keeps her as a spirit watching over spinning and women's household work.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Mokosh appears once in the primary medieval record: as the sixth and only female idol Vladimir installs on the Kiev hill in 980, alongside Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, and Simargl, per the *Russian Primary Chronicle*. The chronicle gives no myth, temple, or festival for her; everything beyond her name and her place in that list is inference or later folklore.

## Two competing etymologies

Philologists disagree on her name's origin. Max Vasmer and others have proposed a link to the Finnic Moksha (a Volga-Finnic people neighboring the early Rus'), implying a borrowed cult; other scholars prefer a native Slavic root *mok- ("wet"), reading her as a moist-earth or mother-earth figure paired conceptually with the sky. Neither theory is settled.

## Folk survival

East Slavic peasant belief recorded by 19th-century ethnographers kept a household spirit called Mokosha or a folk figure tied to spinning, sheep-shearing, and women's domestic ritual, and forbade leaving wool unspun overnight for fear of her displeasure. This is genuine, well-documented folk belief, but it is 19th-century ethnography, not a description of Vladimir's goddess — the line between them cannot be drawn with confidence.

primarySources.text: And he set up idols on the hill [...] and Mokosh.
primarySources.date: entry for 980 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

worship.practices: No medieval festival or rite is recorded for Mokosh. Later East Slavic folk custom (recorded by 19th-century ethnographers, not a pagan-era source) forbade women from spinning wool on her associated day, a taboo folklorists connect to her name but cannot trace back to the pagan period with certainty.

name: Svarog

originalLanguageName.meaning: Probably from a root related to Sanskrit svarga ("heaven", "sky"), suggesting a sky-god origin

description: A sky and fire god known only from a single learned chronicle gloss that equates him with the Greek smith-god Hephaestus and calls the sun-god Dazhbog his son.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Svarog is not among Vladimir's 980 idols. He appears in a gloss inserted into the Hypatian Chronicle's Slavonic translation of John Malalas's *Chronographia*, under the year 1114, where the Greek smith-god Hephaestus is rendered as Svarog, and the sun (identified as Dazhbog) is called "Svarog's son" who "reigned after him." This is a bookish, learned aside by a Christian scribe explaining Greek mythology through a Slavic name he expected his audience to recognize — most historians treat it as evidence for the name and a rough sky/fire association, not as direct testimony to a living cult with its own myths.

## A name, not a narrative

Beyond that single gloss, nothing about Svarog's worship, temples, or festivals survives. His name recurs as an element in Svarozhich ("little Svarog" or "son of Svarog"), the West Slavic fire-and-war god attested independently by Thietmar of Merseburg at Riedegost — whether that patronymic reflects a genuine East-West Slavic theological link, or simply a shared root word for "bright/heaven," is debated rather than settled.

primarySources.text: And after him [Svarog] reigned his son, whose name is the Sun, whom they call Dazhbog [...] Svarog, whom the Egyptians call Hephaestus.
primarySources.source: Hypatian Chronicle, gloss on the Slavonic Chronicle of John Malalas, s.a. 1114 (paraphrase)

worship.practices: No medieval source records a temple, festival, or oath sworn to Svarog directly; everything known about him comes from the single 1114 chronicle gloss identifying him with Hephaestus and naming Dazhbog as his son.

name: Dazhbog

originalLanguageName.meaning: "Giving god" (from dažĭ, "give!", + bogŭ, "god"), commonly read as a solar deity who gives light, warmth, or fortune

description: A sun-and-fortune god among Vladimir's 980 idols, called "son of Svarog" in a separate chronicle gloss and invoked as ancestor of the Rus' people in the medieval epic poem the Tale of Igor's Campaign.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Dazhbog is named fourth among Vladimir's six idols in the *Russian Primary Chronicle*'s account of 980. A separate strand, the Hypatian Chronicle's 1114 gloss on the Slavonic Malalas translation, identifies him with the sun and calls him "son of Svarog." The *Tale of Igor's Campaign* (*Slovo o polku Igoreve*), a medieval poem describing a failed 1185 Rus' military campaign whose manuscript and dating have drawn scholarly debate, twice calls the Rus' people "Dazhbog's grandsons" — whatever the poem's exact date, it shows the name still carried weight as an ancestral, poetic figure for the audience it was written for.

## Reading the sources together

The 980 list, the 1114 gloss, and the *Tale* come from three different kinds of text — a political chronicle entry, a scribal aside translating Greek myth, and an epic poem — and none of them narrate an actual myth about Dazhbog's deeds. What can be said with confidence is that he was one of the state cult's official gods and that his name endured afterward as a literary figure of speech for the Rus' as a people.
originStory: The only genealogical claim about Dazhbog comes from the Hypatian Chronicle's 1114 gloss on Malalas, which says he reigned as the sun after his father Svarog; no birth or creation narrative survives.

primarySources.text: And he set up idols [...] Dazhbog [...] on the hill outside the palace.
primarySources.date: entry for 980 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

primarySources.text: Now the sons of Rus' set out [...] in the age of Troyan, in the years of Yaroslav, in the campaigns of Oleg [...] we, the grandsons of Dazhbog.
primarySources.source: Tale of Igor's Campaign (Slovo o polku Igoreve), paraphrase
primarySources.date: describing events of 1185; surviving manuscript copy 16th c., first printed 1800

worship.practices: Named among the state idols Vladimir installed in 980 and torn down in 988; no separate festival or shrine is recorded for him specifically. His name persisted afterward as a poetic epithet for the Rus' people ("grandsons of Dazhbog") rather than as an active cult title.

name: Stribog

originalLanguageName.meaning: Disputed; possibly "the god who spreads/disperses" (from a root related to "strew"), read as a wind god from the Tale of Igor's Campaign's imagery

description: A wind god among Vladimir's 980 idols, remembered in the Tale of Igor's Campaign as the ancestor of the winds that blow arrows against the poem's defeated Rus' army.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Stribog is named fourth–fifth among Vladimir's six idols in the *Russian Primary Chronicle*'s entry for 980. His function as a wind god rests almost entirely on one striking line in the *Tale of Igor's Campaign*, which calls the winds "Stribog's grandsons," blowing arrows from the sea against Prince Igor's host. Beyond his name in the idol list and that one poetic image, nothing about his myth, temple, or worship survives.

## An inference, held with appropriate caution

The wind association is widely accepted by Slavicists precisely because of how specific and vivid the *Tale*'s image is, but it remains an inference from a single later literary reference rather than a chronicle statement of his domain — the *Primary Chronicle* itself never says what Stribog governed.

primarySources.text: And he set up idols [...] Stribog [...] on the hill outside the palace.
primarySources.date: entry for 980 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

primarySources.text: Behold, the winds, Stribog's grandsons, blow arrows from the sea upon Igor's brave host.
primarySources.source: Tale of Igor's Campaign (Slovo o polku Igoreve), paraphrase
primarySources.date: describing events of 1185; surviving manuscript copy 16th c., first printed 1800

worship.practices: No medieval source records a rite, temple, or festival for Stribog; he is known only from his place in the 980 idol list and from a single poetic image in the Tale of Igor's Campaign describing the winds as his descendants.

name: Khors

originalLanguageName.meaning: Widely thought to be a loanword from an Iranian language (compare Ossetic xor, "sun"), reflecting Rus' contact with Iranian-speaking steppe peoples

domain: uncertain; possibly the sun or moon
description: One of the most obscure of Vladimir's 980 idols; his name is probably an Iranian loanword, but scholars still dispute whether he was a sun god, a moon god, or something else, especially since Dazhbog already covers the sun.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Khors is named second among Vladimir's six idols in the *Russian Primary Chronicle*'s entry for 980, and appears again in a few later manuscript variants of the *Tale of Igor's Campaign*, where a prince is said to cross Khors's path by night — read by some scholars as implying a lunar association, since crossing the sun's path would make less sense at night.

## An unresolved problem

Most specialists in Slavic philology (following Max Vasmer and later Ivanov and Toporov) treat "Khors" as a borrowing from an Iranian language current among steppe neighbors of the early Rus', related to words for "sun." That creates a puzzle: Dazhbog, standing right next to him in the same 980 list, is also solar. Proposed solutions include Khors as a moon god complementing solar Dazhbog, as a separate solar epithet borrowed through Iranian or Khazar contact, or as a more abstract personification of the sun-disc distinct from Dazhbog's role as "giver." None of these has become a scholarly consensus, and this site does not assign Khors a confident domain beyond what the idol list itself supports.

primarySources.text: And he set up idols [...] Khors [...] on the hill outside the palace.
primarySources.date: entry for 980 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

worship.practices: No medieval source records a rite, temple, or festival for Khors; he is known only from his place in the 980 idol list and a disputed nocturnal reference in some Tale of Igor's Campaign manuscripts, and his function remains an open scholarly question.

name: Simargl

originalLanguageName.meaning: Widely thought to derive from the Iranian mythic bird-dog Simurgh (Avestan Sǎēna), making the name itself a probable loanword

domain: uncertain; possibly plants or a protective/messenger role
symbols: winged dog or bird-dog hybrid, by analogy with the Iranian Simurgh
description: The most obscure of Vladimir's 980 idols; his name almost certainly derives from the Iranian mythic bird-dog Simurgh, but no medieval Slavic source explains what function, if any, he served.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Simargl is named sixth (fifth in some editions) among Vladimir's six idols in the *Russian Primary Chronicle*'s entry for 980, and is not mentioned anywhere else in the medieval East Slavic record — no other chronicle, treaty, or poem names him.

## A borrowed name with no attached story

Philologists including Vasmer and later Ivanov and Toporov derive "Simargl" from the Iranian Simurgh (Avestan *Sǎēna*), a winged, dog-headed guardian creature in Persian myth, presumably transmitted to the Rus' through contact with Iranian-speaking steppe peoples such as the Khazars or Alans. Later Russian folk tradition preserves a creature called Simargl or Pereplut in some regional variants, sometimes described as a winged dog guarding seeds or crops, but the link between that folklore and the 980 idol is speculative. This site does not assign Simargl a confident domain: he may originally have named a creature rather than a personal god at all, and the chronicler may simply have listed a foreign name he found among the idols without fully understanding it.

primarySources.text: And he set up idols [...] Simargl [...] on the hill outside the palace.
primarySources.date: entry for 980 CE; chronicle compiled early 12th c.

worship.practices: No medieval source records any rite, temple, festival, or function for Simargl beyond his bare name in the 980 idol list; even his status as a personal god rather than a mythic creature is disputed by specialists.

name: Svarozhich

originalLanguageName.meaning: "Son of Svarog" or "little Svarog" (patronymic/diminutive form of Svarog)

symbols: a warrior's weapons kept in the shrine
description: The chief god of the West Slavic Redarii, worshipped at a temple in Riedegost and consulted before war through the movements of a sacred horse and lots, known from a German bishop's firsthand account.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Thietmar of Merseburg, a German bishop writing his *Chronicon* in the years before his death in 1018, gives the fullest surviving account of a Slavic pagan temple: a shrine at Riedegost (in the land of the Redarii, part of the Lutici confederation) housing several carved gods, chief among them one he calls Zuarasici, understood by most scholars as a Latinization of Svarozhich, "son of Svarog." Thietmar describes the Redarii consulting this shrine before going to war, using a horse led over crossed spears and reading its steps as an omen. Writing half a century later, Adam of Bremen names the principal god of what appears to be the same or a closely related site "Redigast" (Radogost), leaving it debated among historians whether Svarozhich/Zuarasici and Radogost/Redigast were the same figure under two names, two distinct gods at related sites, or a case of one chronicler confusing a god's name with the name of the town or temple itself.

## Fire and the patronymic problem

The name's "son of Svarog" form has led some scholars to treat Svarozhich as functionally close to Dazhbog (also called "son of Svarog" in the East Slavic tradition), especially given a shared fire association; others read Svarozhich as an independent West Slavic war-and-fire god whose patronymic name need not imply the same theology as the unrelated East Slavic Hypatian gloss. This site treats the connection to Svarog as likely but not proven.

primarySources.text: In the land of the Redarii is a town called Riedegost [...] in it stands nothing but a skillfully made wooden shrine [...] the foremost of the images bears the name Zuarasici, and is honored beyond the rest by all the heathens.
primarySources.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon, Book VI (paraphrase)

temples: The shrine at Riedegost, described by Thietmar as a wooden building carved with images of gods and hung with the horns and weapons of victims and offerings.
worship.practices: Consulted before military campaigns: Thietmar describes a sacred horse led over crossed spears at the shrine, its steps read as a favorable or unfavorable sign, alongside the casting of lots.

name: Svantevit

originalLanguageName.text: Sanctus Vitus / Zvantewith (Latinized by Saxo Grammaticus)
originalLanguageName.meaning: "Holy/mighty lord" (from svet-/svęt-, "holy" or "strong", + vitŭ, "lord")

symbols: four faces looking to the four directions
description: The four-faced war and oracle god of the Rani on the island of Rügen, whose temple at Cape Arkona was the last great pagan shrine on the Baltic coast until the Danes destroyed it in 1168.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

The Danish historian Saxo Grammaticus gives an eyewitness-informed account of Svantevit's temple at Arkona in Book 14 of his *Gesta Danorum* (composed c. 1200–1216), describing a large wooden idol with four heads facing the cardinal directions, a sword, a bow, and a drinking horn held in one hand that priests refilled each year to divine the coming harvest. A sacred white horse, kept in the temple and never ridden except by the god himself (as the priests claimed), was led over crossed spears before military campaigns; its steps were read as an omen, much as Thietmar describes for Svarozhich's cult at Riedegost far to the west.

## Destruction and record

Saxo reports the temple's destruction in 1168 by the Danish king Valdemar I, guided by Bishop Absalon, during a campaign that ended organized paganism among the Rani; the huge idol was reportedly chopped up and burned. Saxo, writing for a Danish royal audience one to two generations later, is not a neutral witness — the conquest and the conversion are the point of his account — but the physical details he gives (the four-faced carving, the horn, the horse ritual) are treated by archaeologists and historians as broadly credible, since they match patterns attested at other West Slavic shrines.

primarySources.text: The statue [...] had four heads on four necks, two facing the chest and two the back [...] in its right hand it held a horn, wrought with various metals, which the priest [...] filled with wine every year, to foretell the coming harvest from how much remained.
primarySources.date: composed c. 1200–1216, describing the temple destroyed in 1168

temples: The great temple at Arkona on Cape Arkona, Rügen, described by Saxo as the principal shrine of the Rani, destroyed in 1168.
festivals: An annual harvest divination rite in which the priest refilled and inspected Svantevit's drinking horn, per Saxo.
worship.practices: A sacred white horse, kept solely for the god's use, was led over crossed spears before war and its gait read as an omen of victory or defeat; a tenth of all war-spoils and plunder was reportedly dedicated to the temple.

name: Triglav

originalLanguageName.meaning: "Three-headed" (tri-, "three", + glava, "head")

domain: sky, earth, and the underworld (per the chroniclers' gloss)
description: The three-headed chief god of pagan Szczecin, whose temple and golden idol were destroyed during Bishop Otto of Bamberg's Christianizing mission of 1124–1128.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

Triglav is known from the *Lives of Otto of Bamberg*, written within a generation of the events they describe by the monks Ebbo (*Vita Ottonis*, c. 1151) and Herbord (*Dialogus de Vita Ottonis*, c. 1158), recounting Otto's mission to convert Pomerania in 1124–1128. Both describe a three-headed idol at Szczecin (Stettin), its heads covered by a golden veil or blindfold that the chroniclers gloss as meaning the god chose to see, hear, and speak no evil of the three realms — sky, earth, and the underworld — the three heads were said to survey. A black, divinatory horse comparable to Svantevit's white one at Arkona is also recorded at Szczecin.

## A missionary's frame

As with Svantevit, the surviving account comes from writers celebrating a bishop's conversion campaign, so the neat symbolic reading of the three heads (sky/earth/underworld, or "see/hear/speak no evil") may be the chroniclers' own interpretive gloss rather than a doctrine the Pomeranians themselves would have stated that way. The idol's fate is recorded precisely: after the temple's destruction, a golden likeness of Triglav's heads was reportedly sent to Pope Honorius II in Rome as proof of the mission's success.

primarySources.text: There was in the city [Szczecin] a triple-headed image, which on the necks joined in one body was called Triglav [...] The priest explained that the great god had three heads because he oversaw three kingdoms, that is, heaven, earth, and the underworld, and that he covered his face with a golden veil, so as not to see or make known the sins of men.

temples: The chief temple at Szczecin, destroyed during Otto of Bamberg's mission of 1124–1128; a related cult is also recorded at Wolgast.
worship.practices: A black horse was kept for divination before military or civic decisions, its refusal to step over crossed spears read as an unfavorable omen, per Ebbo and Herbord's accounts of Szczecin.

name: Chernobog

originalLanguageName.meaning: "Black god" (chrŭnŭ, "black", + bogŭ, "god")

description: A "black god" of misfortune mentioned in exactly one medieval source, a Christian chronicler's brief and moralizing account of a feast toast; the paired "white god" Belobog appears only in much later sources, and most of what is said about Chernobog today goes beyond the evidence.
detailedBio:
## A single, thin source

Everything known about Chernobog comes from one passage in Helmold of Bosau's *Chronica Slavorum* (Book I, chapter 52, written c. 1168), describing Slavs at a shared feast passing a cup and speaking words invoking, as Helmold reports it, a good god and an evil one, "which in their language they call Zcerneboch, that is, the black god." Helmold states plainly that the Slavs believed good fortune came from the good god and misfortune was dispensed by the black one, and that they preferred to curse the evil god than to praise the good one. No other medieval writer, chronicle, or inscription mentions Chernobog.

## What this site will not add

A popularly repeated "White God," Belobog, presented as Chernobog's opposite number, appears nowhere in Helmold or any other medieval source; the name is first attested only in 18th–19th-century antiquarian and Romantic writing, and modern Rodnovery (Slavic neopagan) material has built an elaborate dualistic cosmology around the pair that has no basis in the medieval record. Because Helmold is a single, late, foreign-authored, and explicitly moralizing witness, some historians have also asked whether his account reflects genuine Slavic dualism or a Christian writer's own framework of good and evil projected onto an unfamiliar toast. This site presents Chernobog only as far as Helmold's own words support, and no further.

primarySources.text: Among the various forms of their idols [...] the Slavs also have a strange delusion: at feasts and carousals they pass around a bowl over which they utter words, I will not say of consecration but of execration, in the name of the gods, of the good one as well as the bad one, professing that all good fortune is arranged by the good god, adversity by the bad one; hence also in their language they call the bad god Zcerneboch, that is, the black god.
primarySources.source: Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum, Book I, ch. 52 (paraphrase)

worship.practices: The only recorded practice is a feast-toast rite described by Helmold, in which a shared cup is passed while words are spoken invoking both a good god and Chernobog; no temple, idol, or dedicated festival is recorded anywhere else for him.

name: Sky Woman
description: The woman who falls from the Sky World through a hole torn open when a great tree is uprooted, and is caught and set on the back of the Great Turtle, whose back becomes Turtle Island.
detailedBio:
## Attestation and variation

Sky Woman's fall is the opening event of Haudenosaunee cosmological tradition, recorded in detail by J.N.B. Hewitt (Tuscarora) in *Iroquoian Cosmology* from Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk tellers, and by Arthur C. Parker (Seneca) in *Seneca Myths and Folk Tales* (1923). Tellings agree on the core shape, a woman falls from a torn-open sky, is slowed by waterfowl, and is set on a turtle whose back grows into the earth, but differ on why she fell (an uprooted tree, a jealous husband, curiosity about the hole of light), which animal succeeds at diving for the mud that becomes land, and other particulars. This site follows Hewitt and Parker in treating these as genuine regional and individual variants rather than errors to be corrected into one master version.

## Grandmother of the Twins

Sky Woman's daughter is born on the new earth, and that daughter, in most tellings, dies giving birth to twin sons, Sapling and Flint, whom Sky Woman then raises. This detail, that the Twins are her grandsons rather than sons, is consistent across the Parker and Hewitt recordings, though different tellers give the daughter different fates and different explanations for how she conceived.

## Not a dated story

Haudenosaunee tradition presents this account in the present tense, as an ongoing description of how the world came to be, not as a chronicle with a year attached; this site follows that framing rather than assigning it a calendar date.

primarySources.text: A composite account drawing on Hewitt's recorded Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk tellings of Sky Woman's fall and the founding of Turtle Island.
primarySources.source: J.N.B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, Bureau of American Ethnology Annual Reports 21 and 43

primarySources.text: A Seneca telling of the sky woman's fall and the diving animals, recorded from named Seneca tellers.
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

worship.practices: Sky Woman's story is told as part of Haudenosaunee oral tradition rather than marked by a specific festival or temple; this site does not describe any ceremony associated with her, in keeping with the guidance of the sources used here.

name: Sapling

originalLanguageName.meaning: "He Holds Up the Sky," one of several nation-specific names for this twin; called Sapling or Skyholder in many English retellings

symbols: corn, beans, and squash (the Three Sisters)
description: The good-minded twin grandson of Sky Woman, who in Haudenosaunee tradition shapes the world's fertile land, food plants, and easy rivers, opposite his hard-minded brother Flint.
detailedBio:
## A name that varies by nation

What English retellings often call Sapling or Skyholder is given different names by different Haudenosaunee nations and tellers: the Mohawk name Teharonhiawagon ("He Holds Up the Sky") is recorded by several 19th- and 20th-century sources, while Arthur C. Parker's Seneca tellers use Djuskaha and other terms. This site uses Sapling and Skyholder as the most common English forms while naming the Mohawk term as one nation's own name for him, not the only correct one.

## The Twins' contest

After their grandmother Sky Woman raises them, Sapling and his brother Flint shape the features of the earth in opposite ways, one making it fertile, temperate, and easy to live in, the other making it difficult: mountains, rapids, and thorns, in some tellings, or dangerous creatures in others. Parker and Hewitt's recorded tellers differ on how their rivalry resolves, some describing a contest Sapling wins decisively, others describing an ongoing balance between the two rather than one twin's defeat. This site follows its sources in presenting that as unresolved variation, not a single correct ending.

primarySources.text: A Seneca telling of the Twins' birth and their shaping of the world's features, recorded from named tellers.
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

primarySources.text: A comparative record of Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk tellings of the Twins' contest.
primarySources.source: J.N.B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, Bureau of American Ethnology Annual Reports 21 and 43

worship.practices: No specific ceremony for Sapling is described in the public sources this site draws on; the Three Sisters (corn, beans, and squash) that many tellings credit to him remain a living agricultural and ceremonial staple among Haudenosaunee communities today, a continuity this site notes without describing any restricted ceremony attached to it.

name: Flint

originalLanguageName.meaning: Commonly glossed "flint" or "the hard/icy one"

description: The hard-minded twin grandson of Sky Woman, born in a way that costs their mother's life, who in Haudenosaunee tradition shapes the earth's difficult features in contest with his brother Sapling.
detailedBio:
## A difficult birth, a contested ending

In most recorded tellings, Flint is born after his brother Sapling in a way described as unusually violent, some tellers say he forces his way out rather than being born in the ordinary manner, and this birth costs their mother's life, which is why Sky Woman raises the Twins herself. From there, Flint shapes the parts of the world that make life harder: difficult terrain, dangerous animals, or winter, depending on the teller. Hewitt's and Parker's recorded tellers do not agree on how the brothers' rivalry ends, and this site does not present one outcome as final.

## Not a simple villain

Haudenosaunee tellings recorded by Parker and Hewitt generally do not cast Flint as evil in the way a folkloric devil figure is; he represents difficulty and hardship as a genuine part of the world's balance, set against Sapling's ease and abundance, rather than a force to be eliminated outright. This site follows that framing rather than importing an outside good-versus-evil template onto the story.

primarySources.text: A Seneca telling of Flint's birth and his shaping of the world's difficult features, recorded from named tellers.
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

primarySources.text: A comparative record of Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk tellings of the Twins' contest.
primarySources.source: J.N.B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, Bureau of American Ethnology Annual Reports 21 and 43

worship.practices: No specific ceremony for Flint is described in the public sources this site draws on.

name: Great Turtle
symbols: the turtle's shell (often read as marking the seasons or lands)
description: The turtle on whose back Sky Woman is set as she falls from the Sky World, and whose back, built up with earth by other animals, becomes Turtle Island, the Haudenosaunee name for the continent.
detailedBio:
## Attestation

The Great Turtle appears in Haudenosaunee cosmological tradition as recorded by Hewitt and Parker: after Sky Woman falls and is slowed by waterfowl, the animals of the primordial waters debate who can bear her weight, and the turtle volunteers his back; another animal (muskrat, in many Seneca and Onondaga tellings, though other tellers name other divers) succeeds in bringing up mud from the depths to spread across the turtle's back, which grows into the earth. "Turtle Island" remains a name Haudenosaunee people and other Indigenous nations across North America use for the continent today, a living use of the story's image, not only a historical reference.

## Variation across tellers

Which animal dives for the mud, how many attempts fail before one succeeds, and exactly how large the resulting land becomes vary between the Seneca tellers Parker recorded and the Onondaga and Mohawk tellers Hewitt recorded. This site does not resolve those differences into a single version.

primarySources.text: A Seneca telling of the diving animals and the growth of the earth on the turtle's back, recorded from named tellers.
primarySources.source: Arthur C. Parker, Seneca Myths and Folk Tales

primarySources.text: A comparative record of Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk tellings of the earth-diver episode.
primarySources.source: J.N.B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, Bureau of American Ethnology Annual Reports 21 and 43

worship.practices: No specific ceremony is described in the public sources this site draws on.

name: Raven

originalLanguageName.meaning: "Raven"; the two Haida forms reflect the language's northern and southern dialects rather than a single standard spelling

description: The central figure of Tlingit and Haida oral tradition, who steals daylight from a wealthy old man's nested boxes at the head of the Nass River and, in a Haida telling, coaxes the first people from a clamshell on the beach at Haida Gwaii.
detailedBio:
## Not simply a trickster

As the poet and translator Robert Bringhurst wrote of the Haida telling, Raven "never actually creates anything; he made the world by stealing, exchanging, redistributing, and generally moving things around." Both Tlingit and Haida traditions cast Raven this way: greedy, funny, and self-interested, yet the figure through whom the world's useful and beautiful things (daylight, salmon, the first people) come to be. Raven's stories are told today by Tlingit and Haida people as living oral tradition, and Sealaska Heritage Institute, the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian nations' own cultural institution, publishes Raven stories for public audiences.

## Two nations, two tellings

Raven appears independently in both Tlingit and Haida tradition, and this entry does not merge the two into one story. In the Tlingit telling recorded by John R. Swanton in *Tlingit Myths and Texts* (1909), Raven tricks his way into a wealthy old man's household at the head of the Nass River to steal his boxes of stars, moon, and sun. In a Haida telling recorded by Swanton in *Haida Texts and Myths* (1905) and reinterpreted by the Haida artist Bill Reid in his sculpture *The Raven and the First Men* (1978 to 1980), Raven finds a giant clamshell on the beach at Rose Spit, Haida Gwaii, and coaxes the small beings inside it out to become the first Haida.

## Clan property and public telling

Among the Tlingit, Raven-cycle stories can be clan-owned (at.óow) in their fullest ceremonial form. What this site presents follows the form these stories take in the public retellings published by Sealaska Heritage Institute and in Swanton's and the Dauenhauers' recorded texts, not a claim to ceremonial or clan-specific content.

crossPantheonParallels.note: Both are shapeshifting, morally ambiguous figures whose schemes, rather than any straightforward heroism, reshape the world; the comparison is a common one in popular writing about tricksters, not a claim of historical contact.

primarySources.text: The Tlingit telling of Raven stealing the boxes of stars, moon, and sun from the wealthy old man at the head of the Nass River, recorded at Wrangell.
primarySources.source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts, "Raven, Part I"

primarySources.text: A Haida telling of Raven and the clamshell of the first people, recorded in the Skidegate dialect.
primarySources.source: John R. Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths, Skidegate Dialect

worship.practices: Raven stories continue to be told publicly today, including through Sealaska Heritage Institute's published collections, and are carved and painted on totem poles, house fronts, and regalia across Tlingit and Haida communities; this site does not describe any restricted ceremony connected to Raven.

name: Fog Woman
description: In Tlingit tradition, the daughter of Chief Fog-Over-the-Salmon who marries Raven and creates a run of sockeye salmon, then withdraws it and herself into the water after he mistreats her, explaining why salmon return to Tlingit rivers each year.
detailedBio:
## The story

In this widely told Tlingit story, Raven marries Fog Woman, daughter of a chief called Fog-Over-the-Salmon. She conjures a great abundance of sockeye salmon for Raven and his household, drying more than they can eat. When Raven strikes her in anger or disrespect, depending on the telling, she leaves through the water, and every dried salmon Raven had stored follows her back into the river. Tlingit tellers use the story to explain why salmon return to the region's rivers each year, and it is publicly commemorated in the Chief Johnson totem pole in Ketchikan, Alaska, which depicts Raven, Fog Woman, and salmon.

## A story still told

This is a living story rather than a closed text: it continues to be told by Tlingit families and represented in public Tlingit art, including totem poles raised well into the 20th century. This site presents it as such, not as a historical record with a fixed date of origin.

primarySources.text: A Tlingit telling of Fog Woman's marriage to Raven and the origin of the seasonal salmon run.
primarySources.source: Nora Marks Dauenhauer and Richard Dauenhauer, Haa Shuká, Our Ancestors: Tlingit Oral Narratives

worship.practices: The story is memorialized publicly in Tlingit totem-pole art, including the Chief Johnson pole in Ketchikan, Alaska; this site does not describe any restricted ceremony connected to Fog Woman.

name: Chief Fog-Over-the-Salmon
description: In Tlingit tradition, the father of Fog Woman, named in the story of her marriage to Raven and the origin of the salmon run.
detailedBio:
## A minor but named figure

Chief Fog-Over-the-Salmon appears in the Tlingit Fog Woman story as her father, establishing her as the daughter of a figure connected to fog and salmon abundance before her marriage to Raven. Public retellings of the story, including those associated with Sealaska Heritage Institute and the Alaska Native Knowledge Network, name him this way, though he does not otherwise appear as an independent character with his own separate narrative in the sources this site draws on.

primarySources.text: A Tlingit telling naming Fog Woman as the daughter of Chief Fog-Over-the-Salmon.
primarySources.source: Nora Marks Dauenhauer and Richard Dauenhauer, Haa Shuká, Our Ancestors: Tlingit Oral Narratives

worship.practices: No independent ceremony or practice is recorded for this figure in the public sources this site draws on.

name: Naas Shaak Aankáawu

originalLanguageName.meaning: "Nobleman at the Head of the Nass River"; older ethnographic sources render the name variously, including Naas-sháki Yéil and Naas-sháki Shaan

symbols: the nested boxes of stars, moon, and sun
description: In the Tlingit telling of Raven and the box of daylight, the wealthy old man living at the head of the Nass River who keeps the stars, moon, and sun locked in nested boxes, until Raven tricks his way into his household to steal them.
detailedBio:
## The keeper of daylight

In the Tlingit telling recorded by John R. Swanton, this wealthy old man of the raven lineage owns three boxes, nested one inside another, holding the stars, the moon, and the sun. Raven, wanting light for the world, transforms himself into a hemlock needle and is swallowed by the old man's daughter as she drinks from a stream; she becomes pregnant and gives birth to Raven reborn as the old man's grandson. Doting on this grandson, the old man eventually gives him the box of stars to quiet his crying, and Raven opens it, releasing the stars through the smoke hole; he goes on to obtain the boxes of the moon and finally the sun in the same way, escaping with the sun in his beak.

## A name that varies by source

Different recordings and modern retellings give this figure different exact names and spellings, from Swanton's early transliterations to the modern orthography used by Sealaska Heritage Institute and the Dauenhauers. This site uses "Naas Shaak Aankáawu" ("Nobleman at the Head of the Nass River") as a widely used modern rendering while noting the older forms recorded by Swanton.

primarySources.text: Raven transforms into a hemlock needle to be reborn as the grandson of the wealthy old man at the head of the Nass, who owns the boxes of stars, moon, and sun.
primarySources.source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts, "Raven, Part I"

worship.practices: No independent ceremony is recorded for this figure in the public sources this site draws on; he appears only within the Raven and the box of daylight story.
